title: Too vast for the mind, close enough for every bow
subtitle: Al-Azim: the Magnificent, whose greatness outweighs everything
intro: Al-Azim (الْعَظِيمُ) means The Magnificent, the Tremendous: the One whose greatness has real weight, whose power and majesty no mind can measure, and before whom everything else is light. Muslims repeat it in every bow of prayer. Knowing it shrinks your problems to their real size and turns your bowing into a meeting.

root.sense: From the same root comes 'azm, bone: the dense, solid frame that the whole body rests on and that does not easily break. So 'azim came to mean someone of weight and substance, great in power and standing. The Prophet ﷺ addressed Heraclius in his letter as 'azim of the Romans. Al-Azim is the One whose weight and grandeur are absolute.

row.title: Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent

knowing: Al-Azim is greatness that has weight. It is the magnitude of His being, His power, His knowledge and His command, all at once, beyond what the mind can take in. {idea}You cannot picture Him or measure Him; you can only recognize that everything you can picture is smaller{/idea}. Ayat al-Kursi, the greatest verse of the Quran, ends with Him as the Most High, the Magnificent (2:255), after describing His Kursi extending over the heavens and the earth, whose keeping never tires Him.

Near names differ. Al-Kabir stresses that He is greater than anything you can compare Him to. Al-Aliyy stresses His height and rank above all. Al-Azim stresses weight and magnitude: the sheer tremendousness of who He is. A human can be high in rank but powerless, or powerful but without standing. Allah is both, and Al-Azim captures the substance of it.

Because He is magnificent, everything connected to Him gains weight: His Book is called tremendous, His throne tremendous, His reward tremendous. {trap}What is cut off from Him, however large it looks, is hollow.{/trap}
seeing: Look up on a clear night far from city lights. Billions of stars, and the light from some of them left before humans existed. The Quran's response to such signs is short: so glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent (56:96). After describing creation, the fire, the rain and the human seed in Surah al-Waqi'ah, it asks the reader to declare His magnificence.
The same words close another warning: the person who did not believe in Allah, the Magnificent (69:33). Denial of Him is, at root, a refusal to let anything be bigger than oneself.

And the Prophet ﷺ made it part of every prayer. In Sahih Muslim, he would say in bowing: Subhana Rabbiyal Azim, glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent. Bowing is how people in many cultures show they know someone is above them. In prayer, every Muslim bends before the only One who deserves it.
trusting: Worry inflates things. A missed rent payment, a frightening diagnosis or a family feud can fill the whole sky of your mind. {idea}Remembering Al-Azim puts the sky back where it belongs: your problem has a size, and He has none.{/idea} That does not make the problem unreal. It means it is held inside something infinitely greater, by Someone who carries the heavens without effort.

It also helps with sin. Some people think their sins are too big to be forgiven. {reward}Nothing you have done is heavy beside Al-Azim; His forgiveness is as tremendous as His power.{/reward} Bring Him the weight you cannot carry.
loving: We are drawn to what is magnificent: mountains, oceans, a voice that fills a hall. All of them are faint traces of Al-Azim. {reward}The heart that glimpses His magnificence falls into awe, and the awe turns into love when it realizes the Magnificent One listens to each whispered word in each bow of each prayer.{/reward}
now: Your next prayer, you bow, and your mind is already listing tomorrow's deadlines. Slow down. {idea}Say Subhana Rabbiyal Azim three times as if meaning it for the first time: glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent.{/idea} Let the list shrink beneath His size before you rise.
old: My problems feel like the biggest things in existence.
new: Only Al-Azim is truly vast; every problem has a size, and He holds it.
try: In your next prayer, hold your bowing a little longer than usual and reflect on one sign of His magnificence while you say Subhana Rabbiyal Azim.

dua.text: Ya Azim, glory be to You, my Lord, the Magnificent. Make my heart feel Your greatness, make my worries small beside You, and forgive me with a forgiveness as vast as Your majesty.
dua.note: The Prophet ﷺ glorified Al-Azim in every bowing of prayer (Sahih Muslim), answering the command of 56:96 to glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent.

pairs.why: They close Ayat al-Kursi together (2:255, also 42:4): Al-Aliyy is His height above all, Al-Azim the weight and magnitude of His greatness.
Al-Kabir means greater than anything compared to Him; Al-Azim adds the tremendous substance and majesty of that greatness.
The Magnificent One is also forbearing: though He is Al-Azim, He gives time and does not rush to punish.

faq.a: Al-Azim means The Magnificent or The Tremendous. It describes Allah as the One whose greatness has real weight and substance, whose power, majesty and knowledge are beyond any measure, and before whom everything else is small. It is related to 'azm, bone, the solid frame of the body.

faq.q: Why do we say Subhana Rabbiyal Azim in ruku?
faq.a: Because the Prophet ﷺ glorified Allah this way in bowing, as reported in Sahih Muslim, in line with the Quranic command to glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent (56:96). Bowing expresses humility, and the words declare that only Allah deserves it.

faq.q: What is the difference between Al-Azim and Al-Kabir?
faq.a: Both describe greatness. Al-Kabir stresses that Allah is greater than anything He could be compared to. Al-Azim stresses magnitude and weight, the tremendous grandeur of His being and attributes that the mind cannot encompass. The Quran pairs Al-Azim with Al-Aliyy and Al-Kabir with Al-Aliyy.

faq.q: Where does Al-Azim appear in the Quran?
faq.a: It closes Ayat al-Kursi (2:255) and 42:4, both as the Most High, the Magnificent. It also appears in the command to glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent (56:74, 56:96, 69:52) and in 69:33.
